title: Trump Administration orders CDC to change COVID-19 testing guidelines
description_short: Trump Administration orders CDC to change COVID-19 testing guidelines
description_medium: On August 25, 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention changed its COVID-19 guidance to discourage testing for people without symptoms, even after a known exposure. The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services directed the change, following Donald Trump’s calls to reduce testing. The shift came as schools were reopening and asymptomatic transmission remained a concern.
description_long:
On August 25, 2020, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention revised its COVID-19 testing guidance. People without symptoms were advised not to get tested even if they knew they had been exposed to someone with the virus. The change narrowed the circumstances in which asymptomatic contacts were encouraged to test. The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services directed the revision after Donald Trump had repeatedly argued that the country should conduct fewer tests.

The guidance changed during a period when schools were attempting to reopen and outbreaks were being reported among students and staff. People without symptoms could still transmit the virus, so the new recommendation drew concern about missed infections among exposed contacts. The change concerned federal testing advice; it did not prevent states, clinicians, or individuals from testing people outside the recommended criteria. The available account gives no count of people who went untested and does not measure the effect on infections. It documents a consequential change in federal public-health guidance amid continuing transmission.

description_long:
Maksym Chernyak, a Ukrainian man held at Miami’s Krome Service Processing Center, began vomiting and having seizures before he was taken to a hospital. Medical staff found internal bleeding in his brain and pronounced him brain dead. His death was reported on February 24, 2025. He was the second detainee reported to have died at Krome since Donald Trump’s inauguration on January 20. Genry Donaldo Ruiz-Guillen, a Honduran man, died at the facility on January 23; ICE said he had experienced dizziness and epileptic seizures for months.

Reports about Krome also described detainees sleeping on floors and facing restrictions on phone calls. Those conditions were separate from the medical accounts of Chernyak’s and Ruiz-Guillen’s deaths, and the available information does not establish what caused either death or whether detention conditions contributed. title: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_short: E. Jean Carroll Wins $83.3 Million Defamation Judgment Against Trump
description_medium: On January 26, 2024, a federal jury ordered Donald Trump to pay writer E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million for defaming her. The award followed a 2023 verdict that found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation and awarded Carroll $5 million. The second jury considered Trump’s later denials and attacks on Carroll. Trump rejected the verdict and said he would appeal.
description_long:
A federal jury in New York ordered Donald Trump to pay E. Jean Carroll $83.3 million on January 26, 2024. The case concerned statements Trump made about Carroll after an earlier jury had found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation. That 2023 verdict resulted in a $5 million award. In the later trial, jurors considered whether Trump’s continued denials and attacks on Carroll’s credibility were defamatory and what damages they caused. They awarded Carroll $65 million in punitive damages and $18.3 million in compensatory damages.

The judgment was a civil defamation award, separate from the first case’s $5 million verdict. Judge Lewis Kaplan presided over the proceedings. Trump rejected the decision, said he would appeal, and continued to criticize Carroll publicly after the verdict. The jury’s award reflected its assessment of the harm caused by his post-verdict statements. This account describes the judgment at the time it was issued and does not state the eventual outcome of any appeal.

title: Trump: NJ official accuses Trump of breaking the law to prevent competition
description_short: Trump: NJ official accuses Trump of breaking the law to prevent competition
description_medium: In April 1997, James Kennedy, head of New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, asked the state gaming regulator to investigate Donald Trump. Kennedy alleged that Trump violated a law protecting casino competition by trying to block an Atlantic City tunnel serving a developing casino district. State officials deferred the inquiry while Trump’s lawsuit over the project was pending; no investigation followed after the suit was dismissed.
description_long:
On April 22, 1997, James Kennedy, executive director of New Jersey’s Casino Reinvestment Development Authority, asked the state Division of Gaming Enforcement to investigate Donald Trump. Kennedy alleged that Trump violated a state law intended to preserve competition among casinos by trying to stop a tunnel in Atlantic City. The proposed route would connect the Atlantic City Expressway more directly to the marina district, where hotels and casinos were being developed.

Trump had filed a federal lawsuit in February to block construction. He argued that Kennedy’s agency was funding projects beyond its constitutional remit and accused the state of helping his competitors. The New Jersey Attorney General’s office told the gaming authority not to investigate while the lawsuit was pending. After the case was dismissed, the state did not open an investigation into Kennedy’s allegation. Trump spent more than $500,000 fighting the tunnel by the end of July, according to the contemporaneous account. No state finding established that he broke the law.

title: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_short: Senate Jan 6 Report: Capitol Police Had 14 Intelligence Warnings Before Attack
description_medium: A bipartisan Senate report released in June 2022 found that Capitol Police received at least 14 specific warnings of possible violence before the January 6, 2021 attack. It described failures to act on intelligence across law-enforcement agencies and noted that Trump advisers had received threat briefings. Donald Trump himself received no intelligence briefing that morning because he had not requested one.
description_long:
A bipartisan Senate report released on June 7, 2022, examined intelligence and security preparations for the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. It found that the Capitol Police had received at least 14 specific warnings about possible violence but did not adequately prepare. The report described a wider failure among law-enforcement agencies to coordinate and act on intelligence. It also said senior executive-branch officials, including advisers to President Donald Trump, had been briefed on threats without a corresponding increase in security.

Trump did not receive an intelligence briefing on the morning of January 6 because he had not requested one, according to testimony cited in the account. That distinguishes what his advisers knew from what was briefed directly to him. The Senate findings later informed the House January 6 Committee’s assessment of Trump’s inaction. The report documented warnings, briefing patterns, and security failures; it did not determine individual criminal liability. Its findings show that specific warnings existed before the attack and that agencies failed to respond adequately.

title: Trump: A majority of the Senate votes to convict Trump; Trump is acquitted anyways
description_short: Trump: A majority of the Senate votes to convict Trump; Trump is acquitted anyways
description_medium: On February 13, 2021, the Senate voted 57–43 to convict Donald Trump in his second impeachment trial over the January 6 attack. The majority fell short of the two-thirds threshold required for conviction, so Trump was acquitted. After voting to acquit, Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said Trump bore responsibility for the attack but argued that a former president could not be impeached.
description_long:
On the fifth and final day of Donald Trump’s second Senate impeachment trial, senators voted 57–43 to convict him of inciting the January 6 attack on the Capitol. A majority supported conviction, but the vote fell short of the two-thirds threshold required by the Constitution, so Trump was acquitted. Seven Republicans joined all 50 Democrats in voting to convict.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell voted to acquit and then said Trump was responsible for the attack. McConnell explained that he believed a former president could not be impeached. He had also blocked an earlier effort to begin the trial before Trump left office. The vote ended the Senate proceeding without a conviction, despite the majority in favor. It was Trump’s second Senate acquittal and left Congress without the formal sanction that conviction would have imposed. McConnell’s remarks placed his assessment of Trump’s responsibility alongside his stated constitutional reason for voting against conviction.

title: CHIP and Head Start Attacked: Children's Programs Slashed
description_short: CHIP and Head Start Attacked: Children's Programs Slashed
description_medium: The 2025 budget and reconciliation debate put several children’s programs at risk. A law signed July 4 paused a Medicaid and CHIP enrollment rule for 10 years, while researchers warned that work requirements and state cost changes could threaten children’s coverage. The law signed July 4, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, imposed a 10-year moratorium on a Medicaid and CHIP eligibility and enrollment rule that had streamlined enrollment for more than 37 million children. Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families found that 21 states covering lawfully residing immigrant children through separate CHIP programs could face a doubled state share of costs unless they dropped coverage. The Commonwealth Fund estimated that one in five children could be at risk of losing Medicaid coverage under the bill’s work requirements.

Separately, a draft Health and Human Services budget from the Trump administration in April proposed eliminating all federal funding for Head Start, an early education program serving more than 500,000 children. The proposal said Congress should not continue funding the program. A draft budget is not an enacted cut, and the cited estimates describe potential coverage risks rather than confirmed losses. The enacted enrollment-rule moratorium and the proposed Head Start elimination had different legal status, though both raised concerns for children’s access to health or early-education programs.

The ruling addressed Tennessee’s law under the Equal Protection Clause and came amid a wider wave of state restrictions. The White House also changed the process for selecting press-pool members, taking a role previously held by the independent White House Correspondents’ Association. AP reporters were later turned away from an Oval Office event with El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele. The dispute concerned access to presidential coverage and the government’s response to a news organization’s choice of terminology. The preliminary court finding addressed the likelihood of a First Amendment violation; the appeal remained unresolved in the account.
